title: Make.com GDPR: DPA, Log Retention and Setup (2026)
summary: Make.com requires a data processing agreement to operate under GDPR, but the platform alone doesn't ensure your complete compliance with regulations.
body_markdown:
## When self-hosting or another platform fits, including Activepieces


Stay on Make if its DPA and sub-processor list hold up and your team can maintain the configuration. Move to another hosted vendor or to self-hosting only when residency, control or audit requirements exceed what a processor relationship can give you.


### Options compared on residency, control and effort


The table below sets the three realistic routes side by side, so you can see where responsibility shifts from the vendor to your own team.


Read it as a map of who carries the burden. The cells state what each route can offer, and any row you adopt still needs checking against that vendor's own trust and pricing pages.


Make with DPA Another hosted vendor Self-hosting (Activepieces)


Who hosts Make The vendor You


Region control Set by your plan and zone choice Varies by vendor Wherever you deploy


Certifications stated Listed on Make's trust pages Varies by vendor Activepieces' SOC 2 programme is in progress; pen test summary, DPA and sub-processor list on request; your environment's certifications are your own


Audit logs Per plan Varies by vendor Available in Activepieces


SSO Per plan Varies by vendor SSO and SCIM available in Activepieces


Air-gap No No Yes


Cost basis Subscription Subscription Infrastructure and staff time, plus any enterprise licence


What the table shows is that hosting moves residency from a contractual promise to a technical fact, and the price is operational work. Staying on Make is the Its running cost is documented, and it remains defensible when the DPA is sound.


### Self-hosted approach for data control


If the data stays inside your network, no third-party processor ever receives it. Activepieces has an MIT-licensed core, so a security team can read the code that would sit inside that network before it approves anything, rather than relying on a vendor's description of it.


Teams that can't accept any external processing can run it air-gapped. Those who would rather not operate it can use the managed cloud in an EU or US region.


Expect a review to lean on what the platform states: SSO and SCIM, custom role-based access control and audit logs. Its SOC 2 programme is in progress, and the penetration test summary, DPA and sub-processor list are available on request. Those matter in a review because they let you show who can edit a flow and who ran it.


The air-gapped build is not a cut-down edition: the enterprise list there, including release management, matches the managed cloud pinned to an EU or US region, and MoneyGram and Moneypenny run Activepieces in production.


A security team that rules out every hosted processor therefore gives up none of those controls, though Activepieces makes no HIPAA certification, BAA or ISO certificate claim here, so don't assume one.


**Self-hosting also moves the burden to you** : patching, backups, retention and the security of every connected app become your responsibility.


The enterprise directories (` packages/ee/` ) sit under a separate commercial licence from the MIT core, so confirm which parts you would run, and ask for the security documents and enterprise pricing at[https://www.activepieces.com/sales](https://www.activepieces.com/sales) before you commit.
